title: "You have the right to act, never to the fruit" (2.39–2.53)
hook: the most quoted line in the Gita, the one on posters and in commencement speeches, and what it actually says

segments.voice: Yesterday, duty and the coward: death is certain for the born, there's work that's yours, and win or lose, the same. Your line was do what's yours. What was yours to do? Today, the line. Day one hundred sixty-four.

You've probably met this verse without knowing it. On a poster in a yoga studio. In a graduation speech. On a mug. Something like: do your work, and don't worry about the results. It sounds like a nice bit of stress advice. But it's more demanding, and stranger, than that. It comes in the middle of Krishna's second chapter, just after he tells Arjuna, now I'll teach you a different way of seeing. Listen to what he's doing with it, and why a man on a battlefield needed it more than anyone with a mug.
screen: `ON A POSTER, A MUG, A SPEECH.` → `STRESS ADVICE?` → `STRANGER, AND HARDER.`

segments.voice: Krishna starts with a promise. In this path, he says, no effort is ever lost, and even a little of it protects you from great fear. Then he warns about a certain kind of religion, full of flowery words and rituals performed to get rewards. And then the line itself, chapter two, verse forty-seven. In Sanskrit: karmany evadhikaras te, ma phaleshu kadachana. Your right is to the action alone, never to its fruits. And he keeps going, which the posters usually don't. Ma karma phala hetur bhur. Don't let the fruit be your motive. Ma te sango 'stv akarmani. And don't be attached to not acting, either. That last part matters. Krishna isn't saying care less. He's saying: you get the doing. The results were never yours to own. Plant the tree, water the tree, protect the tree. Whether it fruits, and who eats the fruit, belongs to something larger. And he's not letting Arjuna use that as a reason to sit down, because not acting is just another attachment. Then he gives it a name. Samatvam yoga uchyate. Evenness is called yoga. Steady in success, steady in failure. And two verses later, a second famous definition: yogah karmasu kaushalam. Yoga is skill in action. So yoga, in the Gita, isn't first a posture. It's a way of working: fully, well, and without clutching. For Arjuna, frozen because of what the fight will cost, this is the first way out. He doesn't have to control how it ends. He has to do what's his, well, with his hands open.
screen: `NO EFFORT IS EVER LOST.` · `YOUR RIGHT IS TO THE ACTION ALONE.` · `NOT ATTACHED TO NOT ACTING EITHER.` · `EVENNESS IS YOGA. SKILL IN ACTION.` · then, large: `THE DOING IS YOURS. THE FRUIT ISN'T.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: open your hands. Settle, and breathe. Rest your hands on your knees, palms up. Think of something you're working hard on right now, and how badly you want it to turn out a certain way. Feel the grip of that wanting. Now, keeping the work, let go of the outcome. Your part is the doing: the next email, the next rehearsal, the next honest conversation. The fruit goes wherever it goes. Each time you breathe out, let your palms soften a little more. Stay open. The bell holds the time.
You have the right to act. Karmany evadhikaras te. Your right is to the action alone, never to its fruits.
screen: `YOU HAVE THE RIGHT TO ACT — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the line. Karmany evadhikaras te. Today, do one task as well as you can, then hand the result over and don't check on it. Day one hundred sixty-four.

howItsDone: Gita 2.47, karmany evadhikaras te, is one of the most memorized verses in Hindu life; many Hindus recite it before work or exams, and 2.48 and 2.50 are often quoted as the Gita's definitions of yoga.

match.prompt: what's inside the line — tap the pairs.
pairs: your right is to the action alone

myth: the verse says to stop caring about your work
it says the doing is yours, fully. only the fruit isn't.
the verse also warns against being attached to not acting
ma te sango 'stv akarmani: don't cling to inaction either.
in the Gita, yoga first means a posture
it's called evenness, and skill in action: a way of working.

fork.setup: you're Arjuna. you've just heard your right is to action, never to its fruit. so the result isn't yours. what follows?
options: then I don't have to act at all.
then I act fully, and let go of the result.
then I act only when I'm sure it'll work.
fork.reveal: act fully, and let the result go. Krishna closes the loophole: don't be attached to not acting, either.

original.note: Sanskrit, Gita 2.47: your right is to action alone. karma, action; adhikara, right.

trapdoor: what you thought: don't stress about results.
what it means: the work is fully yours, the result was never yours to own, and not acting is no escape.
what a scholar hears: 2.47 has four parts, and posters quote two. then 2.48 and 2.50 define yoga as evenness and skill in action.

sources.quoted: karmany evadhikaras te, ma phaleshu kadachana

notes: 2.40 paraphrase: 'no effort is lost... even a little of this dharma protects from great fear'. Confirm.

2.42–2.46 on those who delight in the words of the Veda for rewards: summarized as 'a certain kind of religion, full of flowery words and rituals performed to get rewards'. This is internal to Vedic tradition; confirm the wording does not read as a judgment on ritual as such.
The tree image is the script's own, not the Gita's. Confirm.
Recitation of 2.47 before exams/work: common. Confirm.
The index title quotes 'You have the right to act, never to the fruit' as a paraphrase, not from a named translation. Confirm.
Audit (wider sample): the teach said 'yogah karmasu kaushalam' came 'a line later' than 'samatvam yoga uchyate'; it is 2.50, two verses after 2.48. Corrected to 'two verses later'.
